name: Benedict of Nursia

seo.title: St Benedict of Nursia: the Rule, the cave, quotes and feast days
seo.description: Who Benedict of Nursia was, in plain words: the cave, his Rule, Gregory's stories of his miracles, and his feast days East and West.

band.lede: Hermit, abbot, and author of the Rule that Western monks still follow.

picture.alt: Saint Benedict, a tonsured monk in a black habit, kneels at the mouth of his cave with his hands raised, while above him the monk Romanus lowers a basket of bread on a rope and a winged devil flies at the bell on the rock, by the Master of Messkirch
picture.credit: Saint Benedict at Prayer, Master of Messkirch, about 1530. Staatsgalerie Stuttgart. Public domain.
picture.creator: Master of Messkirch

card.line: Hermit, abbot, and author of the Rule that Western monks still follow.

filters.alias: norcia monte cassino subiaco benedictine rule

who: Benedict was born at Nursia in Italy, about 480, and sent to Rome to study. He left the schools to live alone in a cave at Subiaco. Monks gathered round him, and he later built the monastery of Monte Cassino. There he wrote a short Rule for monks, which Western monks and nuns still follow.

roles.name: Student
roles.line: Sent to Rome, left the schools

lines: At Subiaco, fed by the monk Romanus
No one else knew where he was
A head and twelve monks in each
Any order will do, if all are sung
The old monks sang them all in a day

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 480, in the province of Nursia, today **Norcia in Umbria, Italy**. His family was well born, says Gregory.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: He was sent to **Rome** to study. He left the schools as a young man, about 500.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: At **Monte Cassino**, of a fever, about 547. Some say 543. Tradition gives the day as **21 March**. Gregory gives no date.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: At Monte Cassino, in the chapel of St John he built on Apollo's altar. He lay in the grave he had made for himself, where he had buried his sister Scholastica.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Benedict of Norcia**. The **Father of Western Monasticism**, in the Church of England's calendar. **Venerable Benedict of Nursia**, in the Orthodox churches.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans. The ELCA remembers him too.

facts.label: Patron of
facts.text: **Europe**, named by Pope Paul VI in 1964. Britannica adds students, monks and nuns. It says he is also called on against poisoning and kidney disease.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: An abbot in a black habit, with a book and a staff. Often a broken cup, and a raven with a loaf: the two times he was poisoned. In an Eastern fresco at Peć, an old monk with a white beard and a scroll.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: One book: his **Rule** for monks, in a prologue and 73 short chapters.

portrait.alt: A fresco on a dark wall: Saint Benedict, a monk with a white beard and a gold halo, in a brown cloak over a pale habit, holds an open scroll with Slavonic writing; above him the words 'Holy Benedict' in Church Slavonic
portrait.credit: Saint Benedict, fresco. Patriarchate of Peć, Kosovo. Public domain.
portrait.caption: A fresco at the Patriarchate of Peć, a Serbian Orthodox monastery in Kosovo. The Slavonic words over him read “Holy Benedict”. Public domain.

typeNote: Confident here means steady and hard to rattle, never proud. His face also stands for The Shepherd, one of the test's seven roles: the one who keeps a community together.

west.text: In the **1916 Roman Martyrology**, the old day of his death. It was the **Catholic** feast until 1969.
**Catholic** memorial. Also a Lesser Festival in the **Church of England**, and kept by the **Episcopal Church** and Lutherans in the **ELCA**. Not in the **Missouri Synod**'s calendar.

east.text: **Greek** churches and the **OCA**, as Venerable Benedict of Nursia.
**Russian Church**, which keeps 14 March on the old calendar.

feasts.note: Why two days in the West? Old martyrologies, Bede's among them, give 21 March as the day of his death. But that day always falls in Lent. So in 1969 Rome moved his memorial to 11 July. Books written in Gaul already kept a July feast for him at the end of the 8th century, though where it came from is not known. The East has kept 14 March since the 10th century. Churches on the old calendar keep it 13 days later, on 27 March.

traits.title: hard to rattle
traits.text: A Goth named Galla killed any monk or priest who came before him. He drove a farmer to the abbey with his arms tied, and shouted at Benedict to get up and hand over the man's money. Benedict looked up from his book, and the ropes fell from the farmer's arms. Galla fell at his feet. Yet Benedict “rose not up from his reading”. He had his monks give the Goth something to eat, and told him to stop his cruelty.

traits.title: calm under attack
traits.text: When his monks tried to poison him, he stood up “with a mild countenance and quiet mind” and asked God to forgive them. When a jealous priest sent him a poisoned loaf, Gregory says he “was far more sorry for him than grieved for himself”. When that priest died, he wept.

traits.title: roused to anger
traits.text: Gregory does not hide his anger. In a famine his cellarer held back the last glass of oil from a man who asked for it. Benedict, “in an anger”, had it thrown out of the window, “to the end that nothing might remain in the Abbey contrary to obedience”. Once, worn out by a monk who kept asking to leave, he told him in anger to go.

traits.title: sad, not tearful
traits.text: His friend Theoprobus once found him weeping bitterly, and waited a long time for him to stop. That was not his way, says Gregory, “for the man of God used not in his prayers to weep, but rather to be sad”. He was weeping because he foresaw his abbey sacked. He had begged God to spare the monks' lives.

traits.title: gave the credit away
traits.text: When Maurus ran across the lake to save young Placidus, Benedict put it down to Maurus's obedience, not to his own merits. When a father begged him to raise his dead son, he first protested: “such miracles are not for us to work, but for the blessed Apostles”.

traits.title: moderate on purpose
traits.text: He wanted a rule a beginner could keep, and he allowed his monks a little wine. He tells the abbot to arrange everything so “that the strong may still have something to desire and the weak may not draw back”.

cite.text: Rule of St Benedict, chapters 40, 64 and 73

traits.title: ran from praise
traits.text: His first miracle, the mended sieve, made him famous in the village. So he slipped away from his nurse and went alone into the wild. He wanted “rather to be wearied with labour for God's sake, than to be exalted with transitory commendation”.

said.lede: No one who knew him wrote his life. Gregory the Great wrote it about fifty years after his death, from what four of Benedict's disciples told him.

quotes.q: …from his younger years, carried always the mind of an old man; for his age was inferior to his virtue.
quotes.who: Gregory the Great, at the start of the Life

quotes.q: …the holy man could not otherwise teach, than himself lived.
quotes.who: Gregory the Great, on the Rule. To know how Benedict lived, he says, read it.

quotes.q: This one man was full of the spirit of all good men.
quotes.who: Peter the deacon, Gregory's listener. In Benedict's wonders he saw Moses, Elisha, Peter, Elijah and David.

moments.title: Walking out of school
moments.text: He was sent to Rome to study. There he saw many students slide into loose living. So he gave up his books and his father's house, to serve God alone. His nurse would not let him go without her, and they stayed at Enfide, today Affile. Gregory says he left “instructed with learned ignorance, and furnished with unlearned wisdom”.

moments.title: The bread on a rope
moments.text: He slipped away from his nurse to a narrow cave at Subiaco, almost forty miles from Rome. On the way he met a monk, Romanus, who gave him a monk's habit and kept his secret. For three years only Romanus knew where he was. Romanus saved loaves from his own rations and let them down over the cliff on a long rope. He tied a little bell to the rope, so Benedict would hear the bread coming. One day the devil threw a stone and broke the bell. Romanus kept coming anyway.

moments.title: He did not know it was Easter
moments.text: The Lord told a priest far away that he had a feast ready while His servant went hungry. The priest searched the hills and found the cave. After they prayed, he said it was time to eat, because it was Easter. Benedict had lost count of the days. He answered, “I know that it is Easter with me and a great feast, having found so much favour at God's hands as this day to enjoy your company”. Soon after, shepherds found him. He was dressed in skins, and at first they took him for an animal.

moments.title: The nettles
moments.text: One day the memory of a woman he had once seen came back to him. The temptation grew so strong that he nearly left the wilderness. Instead he threw off his clothes and rolled in a patch of briars and nettles until his skin was torn. Gregory writes, “and so by the wounds of his body, he cured the wounds of his soul”. Benedict later told his disciples he was never tempted that way again.

moments.title: The poisoned wine
moments.text: The monks of a nearby monastery lost their abbot and begged Benedict to take his place. He warned them that their ways and his would never agree, but at last he gave in. When he held them to a strict life, they put poison in his wine. He made the sign of the cross over the glass, and it broke as if hit by a stone. He told them, “Go your ways, and seek ye out some other father suitable to your own conditions”. Then he went back to the wilderness he loved.

moments.title: Twelve houses of twelve
moments.text: So many came to him that he built twelve monasteries, with a head and twelve monks in each. He kept a few monks with him, to teach them himself. Roman nobles brought him their sons to raise. Among them were Maurus, a young man, and Placidus, still a small boy.

moments.title: The jealous priest
moments.text: Florentius, a priest nearby, envied him. He spoke against him and sent him a poisoned loaf. Then he sent seven naked young women to dance in the monks' yard. Benedict feared for his young monks, so he left with a few of them. Gregory says “he gave place to envy”. Soon after, Florentius's room collapsed and killed him, though the rest of the house stood. Benedict wept. He gave Maurus, who sent him the news gladly, a penance for rejoicing.

moments.title: Apollo's hill
moments.text: On the mountain above the town of Cassino stood an old temple. Country people still worshipped Apollo there, and offered sacrifice in the woods around it. Benedict smashed the idol, overturned the altar and burned the woods. In the temple he built a chapel of St Martin, and where the altar had stood, a chapel of St John. He preached until the people around became Christians. Then, Gregory says, the devil came to him in plain sight, raging. Calling him Blessed Benedict got no answer, so he cried, “Cursed Benedict, and not blessed: what hast thou to do with me?” Here Benedict built the monastery where he lived to the end.

moments.title: The king in disguise
moments.text: Totila, king of the Goths, wanted to test whether Benedict was really a prophet. He dressed one of his guards, Riggo, in his own royal robes and sent him with a train of courtiers. As soon as Riggo came near, Benedict called out, “Put off, my good son, put off that apparel, for that which thou hast on, is none of thine.” Riggo fell to the ground. Then Totila came himself. He dared not come near, and threw himself on the ground. Benedict went to him, lifted him up and told him, “Much wickedness do you daily commit, and many great sins have you done: now at length give over your sinful life.” He foretold that Totila would reign nine years and die in the tenth. From then on, says Gregory, the king was less cruel.

moments.title: His sister's storm
moments.text: His sister Scholastica came once a year, and they met on the abbey’s land, just outside its gate. One evening she begged him to stay the night and talk of heaven. He refused, because he could not spend a night outside his abbey. The sky was clear. She laid her head on her hands and prayed, and a storm broke so hard that no one could step outside. “God forgive you, what have you done?” he said. She answered, “I desired you to stay, and you would not hear me, I have desired our good Lord, and He hath vouchsafed to grant my petition”. They talked all night. Gregory's verdict: “of right she did more which loved more”. Three days later Benedict saw her soul rise to heaven like a dove.

moments.title: The whole world in one ray
moments.text: Praying at his window before dawn, he saw a light brighter than day. As he told it later, “the whole world, gathered as it were together under one beam of the sun, was presented before his eyes”. In the light he saw the soul of Germanus, bishop of Capua, carried to heaven in a ball of fire. He had a man sent to Capua. Germanus had died at that very hour.

miracles.lede: Gregory's book on Benedict is a book of wonders. Almost every one of its 38 short chapters tells a miracle, a prophecy or a vision. At the start he says where his stories came from.

pledge.q: All the notable things and acts of his life I could not learn; but those few, which I mind now to report, I had by the relation of four of his disciples.
pledge.who: Gregory the Great. He names them: the next two abbots of Monte Cassino, an abbot in Rome, and the abbot of Subiaco.

items.title: The boy under the wall
items.text: The monks were raising a wall. The devil told Benedict, mocking him, that he was on his way to them. Benedict sent a warning, but the wall came down and killed a young boy monk, the son of a town councillor. The monks carried him to Benedict in a sack, his bones broken. Benedict had him laid where he himself used to pray. He sent everyone out and shut the door. Then he prayed harder than he ever had.
items.quote: for the very same hour he made him sound, and as lively as ever he was before; and sent him again to his former work
items.witness: Benedict sent him straight back to help the monks finish the same wall.

items.title: The farmer's son
items.text: A farmer laid his dead son at the abbey gate and ran to find Benedict, crying, “Give me my son, give me my son!” At first Benedict protested that such miracles were for the apostles. The man swore he would not leave. So Benedict knelt and lay on the child's body. Then he rose, held up his hands to heaven and prayed. He took the child by the hand and gave him back to his father alive.
items.quote: Behold not, O Lord, my sins, but the faith of this man, that desireth to have his son raised to life, and restore that soul to the body, which Thou hast taken away.
items.witness: Everyone there saw the child's body begin “in strange manner to pant and shake”.

note.text: Gregory tells the second as a miracle won by prayer, not worked by his own power: “this miracle was not in his own power, for which prostrate upon the ground he prayed so earnestly”.

more.title: The mended sieve
more.text: At Enfide his nurse borrowed a sieve, and it broke in two. She wept, because it was not hers. He took the pieces and prayed with tears, and it was whole again. The village hung it over the church door, and it hung there for many years.
more.quote: that the place could not be seen where before it was broken

more.title: Water on the mountain
more.text: Three of his monasteries stood high on a rocky hill, and the monks were tired of the steep climb down to the lake for water. They asked to move. One night he went up the rock with the boy Placidus. He prayed there a long time and left three stones as a mark. He told the monks to dig there. Water came.
more.quote: doth plentifully, even to this day, spring out and run down from the top to the very bottom of that hill

more.title: The blade from the lake
more.text: A humble Goth who had become a monk was clearing briars by the lake. The iron head of his hook flew off into deep water. Benedict put the handle into the lake. The iron rose from the bottom and slid back onto it. He handed it back with these words.
more.quote: Behold here is thy bill again, work on, and be sad no more.

more.title: Maurus on the water
more.text: Young Placidus fell into the lake while fetching water, and the current carried him out. Benedict, in his cell, knew at once and sent Maurus running. Maurus ran out over the water and pulled the boy back by the hair. Only on the shore did he see what he had done. Benedict said it was Maurus's obedience. Maurus said it was Benedict's command. Placidus settled it: he had seen the abbot's cloak over his head as he was pulled out.
more.quote: A strange thing, and since the time of Peter the Apostle never heard of!

more.title: The raven and the loaf
more.text: A raven came from the woods every day at dinner to take bread from his hand. The day the poisoned loaf came from Florentius, Benedict threw it to the bird. The raven hopped and cried, as if it wanted to obey and could not. At last it carried the loaf off, and came back three hours later for its usual bread.
more.quote: In the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, take up that loaf, and leave it in some such place where no man may find it.

more.title: Seeing from afar
more.text: Monks came back from an errand and said they had not eaten outside. He told them whose house they had eaten in, what they ate and how many cups they drank. He warned a lay brother not to drink from the flask of wine he had hidden in a bush, and a snake came out of it. He knew of napkins a monk had tucked into his habit.
more.quote: Why do you tell an untruth? For did you not go into such a woman's house?

more.title: Flour in a famine
more.text: In a famine the abbey was down to five loaves. He told his gloomy monks, “Indeed, today some want there is, but tomorrow you shall have plenty”. The next day the flour was there. No one ever found out who sent it.
more.quote: two hundred bushels of meal was found in sacks before his cell door

more.title: The oil that overflowed
more.text: The glass of oil he had thrown from the window landed on the rocks below unbroken, and not a drop was spilled. He had it given to the man who had asked. Then he prayed with his monks beside an empty barrel. The oil rose until the lid fell off and it ran over the floor.
more.quote: the oil within did so increase, that the cover began to be lifted up

more.title: Two nuns cut off
more.text: Two nuns kept insulting the man who ran their errands. Benedict warned them to mend their tongues or be cut off from communion. They died unchanged, and were buried in the church. Often at Mass their nurse saw them rise from their graves and leave when the deacon sent out those not taking communion. Benedict sent an offering for them, and they were not seen to leave again.
more.quote: Amend your tongues, otherwise I do excommunicate you

more.title: The boy the grave cast out
more.text: A boy monk loved his parents more than he should. He went home without his abbot's blessing. He died the same day. Twice his body was found cast out of its grave. Benedict gave them the Host to lay on his breast, and after that the body stayed buried.
more.quote: Go, and lay with great reverence this our Lord's body upon his breast, and so bury him

doubt.title: Doubted then and now
doubt.text: Gregory marks what he had second-hand. Of one prophecy he writes that Honoratus “saith not that he received it from his own mouth, but that he had it of other monks, which did hear it themselves”. His listener Peter keeps asking how such things can be. Of the great vision Peter says, “neither can I conceive by what means the whole world can be seen of any one man”. In the 1980s the scholar Francis Clark argued that the Dialogues were not Gregory's work, but a forger's, late in the 7th century. The forger, he said, wove in real passages by Gregory. A reviewer of his second book wrote, “Those not convinced by Clark's previous arguments won't, I suspect, be convinced by those offered in his new book.” Britannica judges that “his outline of Benedict's life may be accepted as historical”.

words.note: Benedict wrote one book, his Rule. Lines from it are in Boniface Verheyen's translation. His spoken words come through Gregory the Great, in the English of 1608.

feature.kicker: The first words of his Rule
feature.q: Listen, O my son, to the precepts of thy master, and incline the ear of thy heart.
feature.ctx: In Latin, {la|Obsculta, o fili, praecepta magistri, et inclina aurem cordis tui}.

quotes.q: Let them prefer nothing whatever to Christ, and may He lead us all together to life everlasting.
quotes.who: The last words of his chapter on the good zeal of monks.

quotes.q: Never to despair of God's mercy.
quotes.who: The last of the seventy-three “instruments of good works” in his list.

quotes.q: Not to desire to be called holy before one is; but to be holy first, that one may be truly so called.
It is not in many words, but in the purity of heart and tears of compunction that we are heard.
quotes.who: On prayer. So prayer, he says, should be short.

quotes.q: Although we read that wine is not at all proper for monks, yet, because monks in our times cannot be persuaded of this, let us agree to this, at least, that we do not drink to satiety, but sparingly.
quotes.who: On how much a monk may drink.

quotes.q: That God may be glorified in all things.
quotes.who: Why his monks must sell what they make a little cheaper than others do.

quotes.q: Sign your heart, brother, for what is it that you say? Sign your heart.
quotes.who: To a monk, the son of a great man, who held the candle at his supper and thought himself too good for the job. As Gregory recorded it.

extras.title: His Rule
extras.lede: His one book is short: a prologue and 73 chapters on how monks should live together. Gregory called it “excellent for discretion and also eloquent for the style”. Western monks and nuns still live by it.

items.title: A school for beginners
items.text: He calls his community a school, and he means it for beginners. He ends by calling his book a “least rule written for a beginning”. For more, he sends readers to older books: “the collations of the Fathers, and their institutes and lives, and the rule of our holy Father, Basil”.
items.quote: We are, therefore, about to found a school of the Lord's service, in which we hope to introduce nothing harsh or burdensome.

cite.text: Rule of St Benedict, Prologue and chapter 73

items.title: Prayer, work and reading
items.text: The day runs in turns: prayer together, work with the hands, and reading. The monks sing all 150 psalms every week. The old monks, he sighs, did “in one day what we lukewarm monks should, please God, perform at least in a week”.
items.quote: Idleness is the enemy of the soul; and therefore the brethren ought to be employed in manual labor at certain times, at others, in devout reading.

cite.text: Rule of St Benedict, chapters 18 and 48

items.title: Guests
items.text: Every guest is met by the superior and the monks “with every mark of charity”. They pray together first. The abbot himself pours water on the guest's hands.
items.quote: Let all guests who arrive be received as Christ, because He will say: ‘I was a stranger and you took Me in’.

items.title: Newcomers
items.text: A newcomer is not let in easily. He must keep knocking for four or five days. After two months the Rule is read to him, with the words below. It is read again after six more months, and again after four. Only then may he make his promises before everyone: to stay, to change his ways, and to obey.
items.quote: Behold the law under which thou desirest to combat. If thou canst keep it, enter; if, however, thou canst not, depart freely.

items.title: The abbot
items.text: The abbot is “believed to hold the place of Christ in the monastery”. But before any big decision he must call the whole community together, “because the Lord often revealeth to the younger what is best”. In correcting faults, he must not scrub so hard at the rust that “the vessel be broken”.
items.quote: Let him aim to be loved rather than feared.

cite.text: Rule of St Benedict, chapters 2, 3 and 64

items.title: Punishment
items.text: The Rule is not soft on the stubborn. The abbot may punish the proud and disobedient “at the very first offense with stripes and other bodily punishments”. Boys who cannot understand being shut out are to fast or be beaten. Yet no one may strike a brother without the abbot's leave. And the abbot is to work like a doctor: words first, then Scripture, then shutting out, then the lash. If all of that fails, he turns to one thing stronger, below. If even that fails, the brother is sent away.
items.quote: …what is more potent than all these measures: his own prayer and that of the brethren, that the Lord Who is all-powerful may work a cure in that brother.

cite.text: Rule of St Benedict, chapters 2, 28, 30 and 70

items.title: Where it came from
items.text: He did not write it from nothing. He used the Desert Fathers, Augustine and above all John Cassian, says Britannica. Most scholars now think an anonymous older rule, the Rule of the Master, came first. The Episcopal Church's book of saints puts it plainly: “The major problem for historians is the question of how much of the rule is original.”
items.quote: If this is accepted, about one-third of Benedict's Rule (if the formal liturgical chapters are excluded) is derived from the Master.

myths.claim: His motto was {la|ora et labora}, pray and work, and it is in his Rule.
myths.truth: The words are not in his Rule. Terrence Kardong, a monk who studies it, says the phrase “appears nowhere in Benedictine history before the 19th century”. The Rule does balance prayer, work and reading. Pope Paul VI used the phrase of him in 1964.

cite.text: Terrence Kardong; the Latin Rule; Paul VI, Pacis nuntius

myths.claim: “Always we begin again” is one of his sayings.
myths.truth: It is not in his Rule or in Gregory's Life. It is the title of a modern book by John McQuiston II, who retells the Rule in his own words.

cite.text: The Rule; Dialogues, Book 2; Church Publishing

myths.truth: He founded single monasteries, each standing on its own under its abbot. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls it “his so-called order”. It says a Benedictine joins “a particular household” more than an order.
Gregory calls her only his sister. The twin story is later. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls it “a tradition, which St. Bede accepts”.

myths.claim: The St Benedict medal, with its {la|Vade retro Satana}, comes from him.
myths.truth: Neither the medal nor its prayer is in his Rule or in Gregory. “It is doubtful when the Medal of St. Benedict originated,” says the Catholic Encyclopedia. Its letters were found painted on the walls of Metten abbey in 1647. The medal was first approved in 1741 and 1742.

myths.claim: The briars he rolled in turned into roses.
myths.truth: Gregory says nothing of roses. His editor Gardner says only that the thorns “are piously said to have turned into the roses” still grown at the cave in his day.

cite.text: Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 2, with Gardner's note

myths.claim: 11 July is the day his bones were moved to France.
myths.truth: The Roman calendar of 1969, which moved his memorial to 11 July, says no one knows where the July feast came from. It says only that books from Gaul kept it at the end of the 8th century.

stood.lede: Each line is from his Rule. Three are in old English translations, and one is our own, from the Latin.

circle.name: Scholastica
circle.text: His sister, given to God from childhood. She visited him once a year. Three days after their last night of talk, he saw her soul rise to heaven like a dove, and he buried her in the grave he had made for himself.

circle.name: His nurse
circle.text: She loved him and would not let him leave Rome without her. It was her borrowed sieve he mended. He slipped away from her to go to Subiaco.

circle.name: Romanus
circle.text: A monk from a monastery nearby. He gave Benedict the monk's habit, kept his secret, and fed him in the cave for three years.

circle.name: Maurus and Placidus
circle.text: Two sons of Roman nobles, given to him to raise. Maurus, the elder, became his helper. Placidus was the small boy Maurus pulled from the lake.

circle.name: The monks of his first abbey
circle.text: They begged him to be their abbot, then hated his strictness and poisoned his wine. Their monastery is said to have been at Vicovaro.

cite.text: Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 3, with Gardner's note

circle.name: Florentius
circle.text: A priest nearby who envied him, sent him a poisoned loaf and tried to corrupt his young monks. Benedict left rather than fight, and wept when Florentius died.

circle.name: Totila
circle.text: King of the Goths. He tested Benedict with a servant in his robes, then was rebuked to his face. Gregory's editor Gardner warns that Gregory could not see the Goths fairly: “modern historians depict Totila in far more favourable colours”.

cite.text: Dialogues, Book 2, chapters 14 and 15, with Gardner's note

circle.name: Servandus
circle.text: A deacon and abbot from Campania, and a friend who came often to talk of heaven. He was the one Benedict called to see the light of his great vision.

circle.name: Theoprobus
circle.text: A nobleman who had turned to God on Benedict's advice, and a close friend. He found Benedict weeping over the coming sack of his abbey. On the night of the great vision, he sent the messenger to Capua.

circle.name: Gregory the Great
circle.text: He never met Benedict. He wrote the only early Life of him, about fifty years after his death, and he names the four disciples who told him the stories.

death.big: He died at Monte Cassino about 547, standing up in prayer between his monks.
paras: He told his monks the day he would die, both those with him and those far away. Six days before, he had his grave opened. Then a fever took hold, and it grew worse every day.

On the sixth day he had himself carried into the chapel. He received the Body and Blood of Christ. Then, held up by his disciples, he stood with his hands raised to heaven, and died praying. Gregory records no last words.
He was buried beside his sister, in the chapel of St John he had built where Apollo's altar once stood.

His abbey outlived him. The Lombards later sacked it by night, but every monk's life was spared, as he had foretold. Its church was destroyed in 1944, in the Second World War. Pope Paul VI consecrated it again on 24 October 1964.

later.title: A later story
later.text: Some say monks carried his bones to Fleury in France in the 7th century. Others hold that they never left Monte Cassino. The Catholic Encyclopedia reports both sides. Gregory's editor Gardner calls their place under the high altar “a little uncertain”.

items.k: His death, as Gregory tells it
items.q: Having his weak body holden up betwixt the hands of his disciples, he stood with his own lifted up to heaven, and as he was in that manner praying, he gave up the ghost.
This is the way, by which the beloved servant of God, Benedict, is ascended up to heaven.
items.ctx: That day two monks, one in his cell and one far away, saw the same vision. A road ran east from his cell up to heaven, hung with rich cloths and shining with lamps. A man stood at the top and told them this.

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans count him a saint, and the ELCA remembers him too.

churches.note: A memorial on 11 July. Patron of Europe since 1964
A Lesser Festival in the Church of England, 11 July
ELCA, 11 July. Not in the Missouri Synod's calendar

paras: He did not die a martyr. He lived long before East and West split in 1054, and Greek calendars have kept his day since the 10th century.

In 1964 Pope Paul VI named him principal patron of all Europe. His letter opens with three titles: {la|Pacis nuntius, unitatis effector, civilis cultus magister}. In our translation: messenger of peace, maker of unity, teacher of civilised life.

quotes.q: …the birthday of the holy abbot Benedict, who restored and wonderfully extended in the West the monastic discipline, which was almost destroyed. His life, brilliant in virtues and miracles, was written by pope St. Gregory.

kin.name: Martin of Tours
kin.text: At court everyone flattered the emperor, and the bishops gave way. But “in Martin alone, apostolic authority continued to assert itself.” No one ever saw him angry or excited: “he was always one and the same.” When crowds of visitors grew too much for him, he moved to a hidden cell outside the city.
kin.cite: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin

kin.name: John the Baptist
kin.text: He lived in the wilderness until the day he began to preach. Jesus asked the crowds if they had gone out to see “a reed swaying in the wind”. St Gregory says a reed bends to praise or blame, but “no variety of circumstance bent him from his uprightness”.
kin.cite: Luke 1:80; Matthew 11:7; St Gregory the Great, Homilies on the Gospels

kin.name: Mary of Bethany
kin.text: When Jesus came to their home, her sister Martha was busy with all the preparations. Mary sat at His feet and listened. Jesus said she “has chosen the good portion”.

tidbits.text: Joseph Ratzinger became Pope in 2005 and took the name Benedict, partly with this Benedict in mind. The monk, he said, stands for Europe's unity and its Christian roots.
His monks sleep in their clothes, belted, ready to rise for prayer. But not with their knives on, he adds, in case they are hurt in their dreams.
In Lent each monk gets a book from the library to read straight through. Elders walk round at reading time, to catch anyone idle or chatting instead.
The monk in charge of the stores must treat every pot and possession of the house as if it were a sacred vessel of the altar.
